PRAYER
The Chaplain, the Reverend Margaret
Grun Kibben, offered the following
prayer:
Loving God, we pray Your protection
over us this day. Guard us from anything or anyone who would steal our
affection for You.
It is so easy to get caught up in the
business and the busyness of the day
that our own schedules steal the time
and attention we owe to You.
Things happen, assaulting our sense
of certainty and obscuring our clarity,
that we fail to see You in the midst of
it all guiding us through.
Fear, doubt, and cynicism cloud our
spirits and undermine our desire to remain faithful to Your will for our lives.
Easy answers and lucrative options
lure us away from standing fast by
Your precepts when bearing the strain
of hard choices and difficult decisions.
Heavenly Father, as children dear to
You, on this day and in the living of
our lives, may we keep away from anything that dares to take Your place in
our hearts.
To You, the one true God, we pray.
Amen.

RECOGNIZING
THE
PUNXSUTAWNEY MEMORIAL LIBRARY
(Mr. THOMPSON of Pennsylvania
asked and was given permission to address the House for 1 minute and to revise and extend his remarks.)
Mr. THOMPSON of Pennsylvania.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to recognize
the Punxsutawney Memorial Library
for achieving gold star status from the
Pennsylvania Library Association.
This achievement reflects the library’s commitment to education and
community services.
This status is part of the Pennsylvania Forward initiative, a statewide
effort to help libraries provide resources and information that support
people.
Pennsylvania Forward recognizes
that libraries can position people for
successful careers through reading. The
program offers books centered on basic
literacy, civics, health, and finances.
Mr. Speaker, libraries are an integral
part of our communities. They create a
love for learning. They teach children
essential skills, and they provide a
sense of community for many seniors.
I thank all the librarians and staff
across Pennsylvania who serve children, families, students, and seniors
every day.
Mr. Speaker, I commend the Punxsutawney Memorial Library on this accomplishment. I look forward to learning more about their success in the future.

JUSTICE FOR VICTIMS OF CAMP
LEJEUNE
(Ms. ROSS asked and was given permission to address the House for 1
minute and to revise and extend her remarks.)
Ms. ROSS. Mr. Speaker, I rise today
to demand justice for the veterans and
families affected by water contamination at Camp Lejeune.
It has been over 40 years since toxic
water was discovered on the grounds of
Camp Lejeune, but many victims are
still waiting for our government to do
right by them.
Too many have been left waiting for
help that never arrived. Some have
passed away without ever seeing their
claims adjudicated.
These men and women served our
country honorably, only to suffer from
the devastating illnesses caused by one
of the worst toxic water contamination
disasters in the U.S.
Thousands of Camp Lejeune claims
remain trapped in a backlog in a single
judicial district, leaving veterans and
their families waiting for years for the
justice they were promised.
Just last month, our President decided to dangle the fate of their futures
in front of them as a political ploy.
It is disrespectful. It is disturbing,
and it is time to put politics aside and
deliver swift justice and fair compensation to Camp Lejeune victims.
f

Mr. Speaker, 104 years ago, seven
fearless Black educators at Butler University gathered in segregated Indianapolis, Indiana, to lay the foundation
for the first and only Divine Nine sorority founded on a predominantly
White campus, with a legacy of community enrichment, education, and
Black excellence forever echoed by the
words:
‘‘greater
service,
greater
progress.’’
Sigma Gamma Rho is home to many
firsts—the first Black woman journalist allowed in the White House, the
first Black woman CPA, and the first
African-American person to win an
Oscar.
From the Halls of Capitol Hill, I salute my former colleagues, Corrine
Brown and the first Black woman
mayor of Oakland, Barbara Lee, my
mentor and my shero.
On another note, I want to salute
Commander Jay Beck and his 11 line
brothers for becoming men of Omega
Psi Phi on this day 4 years ago through
Chi Lambda Lambda. I wish a happy
queversary to those gentlemen.

REPAIR AND RENEWAL
(Ms. DEAN of Pennsylvania asked
and was given permission to address
the House for 1 minute and to revise
and extend her remarks.)
Ms. DEAN of Pennsylvania. Mr.
Speaker, last week, the American people issued a resounding rejection of the
chaos, corruption, and cruelty of the
current administration: a reckless war
with Iran, an erratic trade war, inhumane immigration tactics, ripping
apart our social safety net, and degrading our institutions and civil servants.
All of this has sent the cost of living
for your family and mine soaring. All
the while, the President has enriched
himself and his family to the tune of
more than $2 billion.
Last week, the American people said
no more. They gave Democrats a historic majority, a historic chance to
lead, and a charge to bring the cost of
gas and groceries down, to expand
homeownership, to end wars, and to
tell Americans that when they get
sick, they will get care.
Americans rejected the rot and rubble of this administration, and they
embraced the hope for our government
that we can and should work for them.
I believe that, too.
Now is the time to repair and to
renew our public trust in American institutions and our faith for a brighter
tomorrow, for the people.

WITTMAN). Members are reminded to
refrain from engaging in personalities
toward the President.

Ms. FRIEDMAN. Mr. Speaker, I rise
today to honor John Heilman, one of
the founders and the mayor of West
Hollywood, California, who is retiring
after nearly 40 years on the city council.
In 1984, John was elected to West
Hollywood’s very first city council. He
helped to build the city from day one,
and he is one of the longest serving
openly gay elected officials in the
United States of America.
In 1985, in the early years of the
AIDS crisis, John helped to write one
of the Nation’s very first laws banning
discrimination against people living
with HIV and AIDS. He helped to create one of the country’s first domestic
partnership registries, extending recognition and benefits to same-sex couples and senior residents. He cofounded
the West Hollywood Community Housing Corporation to build affordable
housing.
His colleagues have chosen him to
lead as mayor again and again, most
recently just this past year. Along the
way, he spent decades teaching law at
Whittier, Southwestern, USC, and
UCLA, mentoring generations of lawyers. In his final term, he is donating
his entire city council salary to community organizations.
As a former mayor myself, I know
how much of this work happens far
from the cameras and without public
accolades. John has been doing this
work without thanks for four decades,
and I thank him for all of his work and
service.

When I spoke to Dr. V, he shared how
much joy it brings him to watch his
‘‘little eagles,’’ ‘‘aguilitas,’’ grow year
after year. His eyes filled with tears,
and it was clear just how deeply he
loves our children.
‘‘Our
thanks,’’
‘‘muchisimas
gracias,’’ to Dr. V for his vision, his
passion, and his extraordinary contributions. I thank him for inspiring
generations of children.
I give my love to Dr. V and offer
‘‘congrats,’’ ‘‘felicidades,’’ on this welldeserved honor.

HONORING ALFREDO VALENZUELA
(Mrs. GRIJALVA asked and was
given permission to address the House
for 1 minute and to revise and extend
her remarks.)
Mrs. GRIJALVA. Mr. Speaker, I rise
today to honor Dr. Alfredo Valenzuela,
a recipient of the Ray Davies Lifetime
Humanitarian
Achievement
Award
from the Educational Enrichment
Foundation.
Dr. Valenzuela is one of the most deserving people to receive this award.
For over 40 years, Dr. V has dedicated
his life to nurturing young people
through mariachi music, preserving
culture, building confidence through
song and performance, and inspiring
generations of students across southern Arizona, including all of his own
children, who now lead mariachi
groups of their own.
I know firsthand about the impact of
his life’s work. Dr. V was my guitar
teacher when I was 7 years old, and I
am proud to count myself among his
former students, as are my children.
A few years ago, our community
gathered outside Davis-Romero Bilingual School to celebrate the legacy and
unveil a beautiful statue in his honor.
Seeing generations of students come
together, including those now leading
their own mariachi programs, was a
powerful testament to his vision and
dedication.

The SPEAKER pro tempore. Pursuant to House Resolution 1247, the
amendment in the nature of a substitute specified in section 4 of that
resolution, is adopted and the bill, as
amended, is considered read.
The text of the bill, as amended, is as
follows:
H.R. 2102
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in
Congress assembled,
SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

This Act may be cited as the ‘‘Major Richard Star Act’’.
SEC. 2. EXPANSIONS OF ELIGIBILITY TO CERTAIN
MILITARY RETIREES FOR CONCURRENT RECEIPT OF VETERANS’ DISABILITY COMPENSATION AND RETIRED PAY OR COMBAT-RELATED
SPECIAL COMPENSATION.
(a) INCLUSION OF CHAPTER 61 DISABILITY RETIREES WITH FEWER THAN 20 YEARS OF SERVICE WHO ARE ELIGIBLE FOR COMBAT-RELATED
SPECIAL COMPENSATION.—Section 1413a(b)(3)

of title 10, United States Code, is amended—
(1) in subparagraph (A), by striking ‘‘In’’
and inserting ‘‘Subject to subparagraph (B),
in’’; and
(2) in subparagraph (B), by striking ‘‘In the
case of’’ and all that follows and inserting
‘‘The retired pay of an eligible combat-related disabled uniformed services retiree,
who is retired under chapter 61 of this title
with fewer than 20 years of creditable service, is not subject to reduction under sections 5304 and 5305 of title 38.’’.
(b) TECHNICAL AND CONFORMING AMENDMENTS.—
(1) SECTION HEADING.—The heading of section 1414 of such title is amended to read as
follows:
‘‘§ 1414. Members eligible for retired pay who
are also eligible for veterans’ disability
compensation: concurrent receipt.’’.
(2) TABLE OF SECTIONS.—The item relating
to such section 1414 in the table of sections
at the beginning of chapter 71 of such title is
amended to read as follows:
‘‘1414. Members eligible for retired pay who
are also eligible for veterans’
disability compensation: concurrent receipt.’’.
(3) CONFORMING AMENDMENTS REFLECTING
END OF CONCURRENT RECEIPT PHASE-IN PERIOD.—Such section 1414 is further amended—

GENERAL LEAVE

Mr. ROGERS of Alabama. Mr. Speaker, I ask unanimous consent that all
Members have 5 legislative days in
which to revise and extend their remarks and include extraneous material
on H.R. 2102.
The SPEAKER pro tempore. Is there
objection to the request of the gentleman from Alabama?
There was no objection.
Mr. ROGERS of Alabama. Mr. Speaker, I yield myself such time as I may
consume.
Mr. Speaker, I rise in reluctant support of this bill.
Under current law, medically retired
combat veterans with fewer than 20
years of service cannot receive their
full Department of Defense military retirement pay and full Department of
Veterans Affairs disability compensation at the same time.
I agree that law is unfair and unjust,
and I agree that it needs to be fixed as
soon as possible. I just believe we
should pay for it.
Fortunately, Chairmen BOST and
MORAN have found a way to do just
that.
H.R. 9237, the Take Care of America’s
Veterans Act, provides a fiscally responsible approach to fixing this problem while also significantly expanding
other benefits and services available to
our veterans, and yesterday the House
passed it.
So while I support passage of this
bill, I urge the Senate to pass H.R. 9237
and send it to the President.
Mr. Speaker, I reserve the balance of
my time.
Ms. HOULAHAN. Mr. Speaker, I yield
myself such time as I may consume.
Mr. Speaker, almost 7 years after it
was first introduced, the Major Richard

E:\CR\FM\A12NO7.001

H12NOPT1

DMWilson on DSK7X7S144PROD with HOUSE

H6196

Star Act has finally reached the House
floor, and it is about time.
Today, disabled veterans who were
forced to retire because of injuries sustained in combat receive VA disability
compensation, but they do not receive
their full retirement pay.
These veterans served our community and our country with honor, and
they are disabled as a result of their
service. They deserve the full respect,
the full gratitude, and yes, the full benefits of that.
The Major Richard Star Act ensures
that that happens, allowing combat-injured servicemembers who were medically retired before reaching 20 years of
service to receive their full military
pay along with their VA disability
compensation.
The Major Richard Star Act has
more than 340 cosponsors in the House,
and it has broad support from major
veterans organizations, including the
American Legion, the Veterans of Foreign Wars, the Military Officers Association of America, and many more.
The bill directly benefits more than
50,000 veterans and would put money
back into their pockets at a moment
when every dollar counts.
Yesterday, on Veterans Day, we
thanked the brave men and women who
serve our country in uniform, but by
passing the Richard Star Act we can
make sure that our gratitude extends
beyond this week and beyond words
and into every day.
I urge my colleagues to vote ‘‘yes’’
on the Major Richard Star Act and to
finally deliver the support that our Nation’s wounded veterans deserve.
Mr. Speaker, I reserve the balance of
my time.
Mr. ROGERS of Alabama. Mr. Speaker, I reserve the balance of my time.
Ms. HOULAHAN. Mr. Speaker, I yield
3 minutes to the gentlewoman from
New Hampshire (Ms. GOODLANDER), my
dear friend and fellow veteran.
Ms. GOODLANDER. Mr. Speaker, I
rise today in support of the Major
Richard Star Act. This is one of the
most bipartisan bills before the Congress today and for very good reasons.
This bill will right a wrong. It will
correct a grave injustice in the Federal
code. It is going to allow our combatdisabled servicemembers who are medically retired with fewer than 20 years
of service to receive the benefits that
they have earned.
The principle behind this bipartisan
bill is as straightforward as it is important. Military retirement pay and disability compensation are simply not
the same thing: Retirement pay recognizes service rendered; disability compensation recognizes sacrifices endured. America’s combat-disabled veterans should not be forced to choose
between the two.
Under current law, nearly 60,000 combat-injured veterans live with this injustice. I have heard from veterans all
across my home State of New Hampshire who have experienced firsthand
this injustice under law.

For those whose military careers
were cut short by combat-related injuries, this unjust policy only adds to the
burdens that these patriots and their
families already face. No one should
have to choose between the two because combat chose these patriots.
They fulfilled their obligations to our
Nation. They put their lives on the line
for us. This House, this people’s House,
must fulfill our obligations to them.
This bill is about ensuring our veterans receive the benefits that they
have already earned. It is about fairness, it is about honoring service, and
it is about keeping faith with those
who have sacrificed everything in defense of our Nation.
Our combat-disabled veterans have
already paid an extraordinary price for
their service. They should not have to
endure a tax and a financial price as

Bill summary:
H.R. 2102 would permit Chapter 61 retirees—service members who have retired from
the armed forces because of a disability—
with qualifying combat-related disabilities
to receive the full amount of both their military retired pay and their veterans’ disability compensation. (The term Chapter 61
is derived from chapter 61 in title 10 of the
U.S. Code, which established the rules for
disability retirement from military service.)
Except where noted in the Previous CBO
Estimate section, all references in this cost
estimate to H.R. 2102 are to the bill as it
would be amended by H. Res. 1247, a resolution providing for consideration of the bill
(H.R. 2102) to amend title 10, United States
Code, to provide for concurrent receipt of
veterans’ disability compensation and retired pay for disability retirees with combatrelated disabilities, and for other purposes.
Estimated Federal cost: The estimated
budgetary effects of H.R. 2102 are shown in
Table 1. The costs of the legislation fall
within budget functions 050 (national defense), 400 (transportation), 600 (income security), and 950 (undistributed offsetting receipts).

A long-standing federal law prevents most
veterans with service-connected disabilities
from receiving both full military retired pay
and veterans’ disability compensation from
the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).

E:\CR\FM\K12NO7.010

H12NOPT1

DMWilson on DSK7X7S144PROD with HOUSE

H6198

Military retirees who are eligible for disability compensation typically have their retired pay offset dollar-for-dollar by the
amount of their disability compensation.
Two exceptions to that restriction allow
certain retirees to receive both retired pay
and disability compensation:
Under Concurrent Retired and Disability
Pay (CRDP), retirees can receive the full
amount of their retired pay and their disability compensation, subject to certain limits, provided they served for at least 20 years
and have a VA disability rating of at least 50
percent.
Under Combat-Related Special Compensation (CRSC), retirees with qualifying combat-related disabilities receive special compensation up to the amount by which their
military retired pay is offset for disability
compensation, subject to certain limits, but
irrespective of years of service or disability
rating.
For service members who retired based on
disability after fewer than 20 years of service, the CRSC payment plus any residual retirement payment (after applying the disability offset) cannot exceed the amount of
retired pay they would have received based
on their years of service. For retirees who
suffered severe combat-related disabilities
after a short time in the military, that rule
significantly limits the amount they receive
from the military retirement system.
H.R. 2102 would eliminate the disability
offset altogether for combat-disabled military retirees who served fewer than 20 years,
allowing them to receive both the full
amount of retired pay they earned and the
VA disability compensation to which they
are entitled.
According to the DoD Office of the Actuary, in September 2025 the department made
CRSC payments to about 58,000 Chapter 61
retirees who served fewer than 20 years. CBO
expects that number to increase to about
65,000 by 2036.
The average disability offset for those retirees was about $2,275 per month, whereas
the average CRSC payment was about $825
per month. Under H.R. 2102, those disability
retirees would instead receive the full
amount of their retired pay. Thus, they
would receive about $1,450 more each month
in total compensation under the bill than
they will under current law. (Both retired
pay and disability compensation are adjusted
upward based on inflation, so CBO projects
those monthly amounts would increase over
time.) On that basis, CBO estimates that enacting the changes to CRSC would increase
direct spending by almost $13 billion over the
2027–2036 period.
Spending subject to appropriation: DoD
and the USCG make annual accrual payments to the Military Retirement Fund.
Those amounts cover the present value of estimated payments for future retirement benefits—other than concurrent receipt payments—earned during a year. (in addition,
the Treasury makes annual accrual payments into the Military Retirement Fund to
cover the cost of future concurrent receipt
payments.)
Under current law, CBO projects that
DoD’s and USCG’s annual accrual payments
will increase from about $21 billion in 2028 to
about $25 billion in 2036. CBO expects that
under the bill, each of those payments would
grow by 3.6 percent beginning in 2028, as future retirees with combat-related disabilities
are no longer subject to the offset and receive their full retired pay.
On that basis, CBO estimates that implementing H.R. 2102 would increase spending
subject to appropriation by $7 billion over
the 2027–2036 period. Any related spending
would be subject to the appropriation of the
estimated amounts.

Uncertainty: CBO estimates that the number of service members who are retired because of combat-related disabilities will continue to rise over the next decade, albeit at
a slower rate than over the past two decades.
Costs would differ if the number of retirees
changes at a different rate than projected.
For example, if the number of CRSC-eligible
retirees with fewer than 20 years of service
remains at the current level over the next
decade, the estimated increase in direct
spending under the bill would be about $1 billion less than estimated here.
Pay-As-You-Go considerations: The Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010 establishes
budget-reporting and enforcement procedures for legislation affecting direct spending or revenues. The net changes in outlays
that are subject to those pay-as-you-go procedures are shown in Table 1.
Increase in long-term net direct spending
and deficits: CBO estimates that enacting
H.R. 2102 would increase net direct spending
by more than $2.5 billion in each of the four
consecutive 10-year periods beginning in 2037.
CBO estimates that enacting H.R. 2102
would increase on-budget deficits by more
than $5 billion in each of the four consecutive 10–year periods beginning in 2037.
Mandates: The bill contains no intergovernmental or private-sector mandates as defined in the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act.
Previous CBO estimate: On March 23, 2026.
CBO transmitted a cost estimate for H.R.
2102, the Major Richard Star Act, as introduced in the House of Representatives on
March 14, 2025. Both H.R. 2102 as introduced
and H.R. 2102 as amended by H. Res. 1247
would eliminate the disability offset for
Chapter 61 retirees with combat-related disabilities and fewer than 20 years of service.
In addition to that change, H.R. 2102 as introduced would make three other changes to
disability retirement benefits that are not
included in H.R. 2102 as amended by H. Res.
1247. As a result of those differences, the estimated 10–year increase in direct spending
of H.R. 2102 as introduced is significantly
greater than what CBO estimates for H.R.
2102 as amended by H. Res. 1247. Two changes
account for almost all of the $65 billion difference in the cost of the two bills: H.R. 2102
as introduced would make Chapter 61 retirees with fewer than 20 years of service eligible for CRDP and eliminate the cap on the
amount of CRDP that Chapter 61 retirees
with at least 20 years of service can receive.
H.R. 2102 as introduced also would eliminate the disability offset for Chapter 61 retirees with combat-related disabilities and at
least 20 years of service. That change accounts for about $100 million of the difference in the estimated costs.

served, fought, and were wounded on
behalf of us, our Nation, and our freedoms, are left without full care.

the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, Republicans used a procedural trick to
pass a bill that would take benefits
away from veterans.
The best way to honor our veterans
and their families is to ensure they are
receiving all eligible benefits.

safety.

remarkable veterans.

and still I rise and still I rise.

unelected, but still effective, unbought,

Censured but not silenced.
As many of you may recall, I was
censured by this House for my commentary made during a Joint Session
of Congress. That commentary had to
do with a mandate that the President
claims he had, but did not have, to reduce Medicaid, Medicare, and Social
Security in any way.
Those were not my exact words, but
that was why I rose. And, of course, I

the statement of censorship read.
On another occasion, the President
made some very ugly statements about

censured for it, but I was removed.

END-OF-YEAR PRIORITIES

Mr. GRASSLEY. Mr. President, with
the 2026 midterm elections behind us,
Congress must finish its work for this
Congress. On my agenda for Iowans in
the coming weeks, first of all, confirming President Trump’s remaining
judicial nominees to lifetime appointments on the Federal bench, and that
is a responsibility that falls on my
shoulders as chairman of the Judiciary
Committee.
And then obviously, we know it costs
money to shut the government down.
It costs taxpayers money to open the
government up. So keeping the government open beyond the short-term funding bill that expires on December 11
ought to be high on the agenda.
And then passing the National Defense Authorization Act which we have
done for 65 years in a row, and that legislation includes stuff out of my Judiciary Committee that protects kids
who are in danger of the things that
are online.
And then enacting a farm bill that
contains year-round, nationwide E15,
ethanol, and addresses high input costs
that farmers face.
And then passing commonsense permitting reform to unlock the American
infrastructure and reduce government
redtape, and that permitting bill is the
subject of debate right now on the floor
of the U.S. Senate.

Then lastly, something that I have
been involved in for decades—to emphasize the responsibilities that we
have to maintain rural healthcare.
That would include reauthorizing the
Medicare-Dependent and Low-Volume
Hospital Programs, the Rural Community Hospital Demonstration Program,
and a Medicare payment floor for rural
state doctors and clinics.
As we look to the 120th Congress, I
personally congratulated the new
Members of the Iowa Federal delegation on their elections. I look forward
to working with all of those new Members on behalf of the people of Iowa.
The next Congress has a lot to accomplish, and I am ready to work with
these new Members and the Members of
both parties to get things done.
Affordability was front and center in
this election and must be the bipartisan focus next year. Any serious affordability agenda will need to focus on
fiscal sanity and reduce waste, fraud,
and abuse in Federal programs. Our national debt now stands at levels we
have not seen since the end of World
War II while Social Security is projected to become insolvent in just 6
years and Medicare shortly thereafter.
We must find a bipartisan solution to
a very real fiscal crisis that has been
staring Congress in the face for too
long of a time.
I yield the floor.

for the customers in the Washington,

The resulting sewage spill was, the
Washington Post reported, ‘‘one of the
largest spills of untreated wastewater
in U.S. history. Enough raw sewage to
fill 364 Olympic-sized swimming pools
flushed into the Potomac River north
of the nation’s capital, exacting an ecological toll that scientists are still trying to calculate.’’
Why do I bring this up? Well, I will
tell you, because DC Water had first
identified weaknesses in the pipe and
proposed repairs a full 7 years earlier—
7 years earlier—but had been prevented
from starting that by a Federal permitting process that dragged on and on
and on until the pipe suffered a catastrophic failure.
It is an excellent illustration of the
need for permitting reform in this
country. Too often everything from
critical repairs to important new energy projects get bogged down in Federal bureaucracy and are delayed for
not months but years at a time.
And the Washington, DC, sewage spill
is an outstanding example of the potential consequences.
Now, it is important to ensure that
serious environmental concerns are addressed before projects are undertaken,
and it is essential to ensure that the
concerns of local stakeholders, in particular local landowners, are listened
to and that they have a voice in the approval process.
But the Federal permitting process
has gone way beyond that to include
years of senseless delays, often caused
by endless litigation from environmental groups or from Agencies that
are set on studying a project literally
to death.
We have seen those delays happen on
projects with everything from drinking
water and irrigation to building affordable energy sources and better roads
and bridges.
And like in the case of the DC sewage
spill, these delays can even apply to
projects where we are simply replacing
something that has been there for
many years.
These delays all add costs, and those
costs are ultimately paid by families
through things like higher energy
costs, higher gas and diesel prices, and
higher taxes.
The legislation that we are considering today would address that. The Bipartisan American Affordability and
Jobs Act will streamline and reform
the permitting process to ensure that
projects are approved or rejected in a
timely fashion.
This is particularly good news on the
energy front. Needless to say, Americans have been dealing with an elevated cost of living since the early
days of the Biden administration, and
when it comes to affordability, energy
prices affect pretty much everything.
We all know that.
High energy costs don’t just mean
higher gas and electric bills, they mean
higher costs for almost everything.

And one of the best ways to keep prices
of all kinds down is to expand domestic
energy production, everything from oil
and gas to solar and wind to hydropower.
Too often, however, as I said, new energy projects get bogged down in Federal Government bureaucracy and end
up in limbo for years.
Streamlining bureaucracy, by contrast, like the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will do, will
speed up key projects and bring more
jobs and more affordable prices along
with it.
We have talked about what this bill
would do for energy projects, but there
is another kind of project on a lot of
Americans’ minds right now, and that
is data center construction.
Communities in my State of South
Dakota and around our country are
concerned about the movement of data
centers into their communities, in particular, about what their construction
could mean for energy prices.
And I am pleased to report that the
Bipartisan American Affordability and
Jobs Act would enact new protections
for local communities. For starters, it
would require that the data centers
shoulder the energy costs associated
with their operation and construction,
whether that is day-to-day running
costs or the cost of additional infrastructure.
But the legislation doesn’t stop
there. It also provides technical assistance to communities to help them understand and explore the impact a proposed data center would have on their
locality—everything from the economic impact to the energy costs and
infrastructure requirements that would
be associated with the project.
There are a number of other good elements in this bill. I am always particularly invested in what legislation can
do to help farmers and ranchers, which
is the livelihood of our economy in
South Dakota. And I am very pleased
that this bill will extend Clean Water
Act permits for farmers from 5 to 10
years, significantly reducing the frequency with which farmers have to engage with government bureaucracy
with that process.
This legislation will also provide for
faster grazing-related reviews which
will make a real difference to ranchers.
If there is one thing Americans
across our country said in the election
last week, it is that they are hurting
economically.
This bill is one important way that
we can help. Reforming the permitting
process will help advance the kind of
projects that will create new jobs, grow
our economy, and increase wages, and
more American energy development
means a more reliable and affordable
energy supply for American families.
I want to thank Chairmen SHELLEY

COPD AWARENESS MONTH
Mr. CRAPO. Madam President, I join
in recognizing November as Chronic
Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Awareness Month and drawing attention to
the importance of broadening understanding about this disease affecting
far too many Americans.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control
and Prevention reports chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD,
was the fifth leading cause of death in
the United States in 2023, claiming
141,733 American lives. Thirty million
Americans live with COPD, according
to the COPD Action Alliance, while
more than 16 million have been diagnosed, based on National Institutes of
Health data.
COPD is debilitating. It robs a person
of breath and, with it, the ability to
walk across a room, climb a flight of
stairs, or play with a grandchild in the
yard. It is also preventable and treatable and far more manageable when
caught early. Awareness matters.
The COPD Action Alliance also reports the disease impacts some Americans more than others: Rural Americans, including many in Idaho, are
about twice as likely to have COPD as
those living in large cities, and they
often must travel the farthest to receive adequate care; veterans carry a
disproportionate burden as well, as
more than 1 million veterans live with
COPD, about 25 percent of the veteran
population; and first responders, who
breathe in smoke, chemicals and debris
while protecting our communities, face
an elevated risk as well.
I support sustained investment in
COPD research to better align these efforts with research into other diseases
such as cancer and Alzheimer’s. In January 2004, I formed the Congressional
COPD Caucus to raise awareness of
COPD and the threat it poses to our
families and communities. I continue
to cochair this caucus focused on improving outcomes by educating people
about the disease and its challenges
and leading numerous initiatives on behalf of patients experiencing COPD and
other lung diseases.
COPD Awareness Month is an opportunity to reverse the alarming impacts
of COPD and advance the goals of preventive health. Helping more Americans recognize the warning signs, such
as a chronic cough, shortness of breath
during everyday activities, and wheezing or chest tightness, can help catch
the disease early, reduce severity, and

VerDate Sep 11 2014

November 12, 2026

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — SENATE

05:19 Nov 13, 2026

Jkt 079060

save money. Early diagnosis saves lives
and money by keeping patients out of
the emergency room and in their
homes with their families.
To Idahoans and all Americans living
with COPD, your voices are heard in
the U.S. Senate, and COPD is a disease
Congress must not overlook.

REMEMBERING DOLORES HUERTA
Mr. PADILLA. Madam President, few
individuals have done more to advance
the cause of workers’ rights, of women’s rights, or of civil rights in America than Dolores Huerta.
A trailblazer in the labor movement,
California and our entire Nation lost a
remarkable leader when Dolores passed
away last month at the age of 96. But
even as we mourn her loss, we also celebrate the legacy she leaves behind; a
legacy that not only transformed the
labor movement but inspired generations of Americans to stand up and
fight for a more just and equitable future.
It is a legacy that began not in a
union hall or in the fields, but in the
elementary school classroom where, for
a brief time, Dolores worked as a
young teacher.
Growing up in Stockton, CA, Dolores
was always encouraged by her mother
to get involved in her community. But
watching many of her students arriving to school hungry and shoeless as a
20-year-old teacher, Dolores came to
believe that she ‘‘could do more by organizing farm workers than by trying
to teach their hungry children.’’
So, after a year in the classroom, she
made a decision that would change the
course of California history: She left
teaching and dedicated herself to organizing farmworkers in California’s Central Valley.
As a cofounder of the United Farm
Workers, Dolores helped give voice to
thousands of Americans who had spent
generations laboring in the fields without the wages, protections, or dignity
they deserved. During the Delano
Grape Strike, she helped unite farmworkers in the fight for better working
conditions and inspired millions of
Americans to join a nationwide boycott of California-grown grapes.
Before long, what first began as a
struggle in the fields of California soon
grew into a movement that reached
across the country. Together, workers
forced an industry to answer for its
mistreatment of the people whose labor
made it possible. And eventually,
through their efforts, these workers secured a major victory with the adoption of the Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975, California’s first
farm-labor law guaranteeing workers
the right to organize, bargain collectively, and negotiate for better wages
and working conditions.
But for Dolores, the fight for justice
never stopped at the edge of a farmworker’s field. She understood that the
struggles facing working families are
deeply connected and intertwined. The

PO 00000

Frm 00006

Fmt 4624

Sfmt 0634

fight for fair wages is also the fight to
put food on the table and afford a roof
over a family’s head. The fight for
workers’ protections is also the fight
for the ability to care for a loved one
without risking a paycheck and to
work and live free of harassment and
discrimination.
This is what guided Dolores her entire life. Fighting for immigrant’s
rights, she spent months building support for the Immigration Reform and
Control Act of 1986. A member of the
Feminist Majority Foundation, she
championed women’s equality, reproductive freedom, and equal pay. And
through the Dolores Huerta Foundation, she continued empowering communities to fight for better healthcare,
stronger schools, and the right of every
eligible American to vote.
Invaluable fights, all of them. But
fights that also came at tremendous
personal cost as, throughout her life,
Dolores faced sexism, abuse, arrests,
violence, and more. Twenty-two times
she was arrested—most recently at 89
years old. Once, while being arrested
during a 1988 protest, she was beaten so
badly by police that she was left hospitalized with broken ribs and a ruptured spleen.
And this March, at the age of 96, Dolores tapped once more into her bottomless well of courage, to come forward and share another deeply painful
part of her story by exposing the sexual abuse she endured at the hands of
her organizing partner Cesar Chavez.
Even after decades of silence, she refused to let fear stand in the way of the
truth.
Through it all, Dolores never stopped
fighting. She brought extraordinary
courage, resolve, and devotion to her
work, refusing to ever take no for an
answer. It is why her iconic rallying
cry, ‘‘Sı́, se puede’’—Yes, we can—became a call to action for generations of
people who believed a better future was
possible, even when the odds are
stacked against them.
It is no wonder that every April 10,
we celebrate Dolores Huerta Day
throughout California in her honor.
But her legacy is not confined to just 1
day, one State, or one movement. It
lives on in every worker who stands up
for fair treatment, in every woman who
demands an equal voice, in every immigrant who fights for dignity and every
community that comes together demanding change.
Dolores once said, ‘‘Every moment is
an organizing opportunity, every person a potential activist, and every
minute a chance to change the world.’’
Those words were more than a rallying cry. They were a reflection of
who Dolores was and how she lived her
life. From the young teacher who saw
children hungry and ill-clothed, to the
organizer who helped transform an entire industry, to the 96-year-old activist who refused to ever quit speaking
out, Dolores never stopped believing in
the power of ordinary people to bring
about extraordinary change. And she

E:\CR\FM\G12NO6.020

S12NOPT1

November 12, 2026

showed us that a better world does not
simply happen. It is built by those willing to stand together, those willing to
organize, and those willing to demand
something better.
Now, it is up to all of us to carry that
torch forward, to keep organizing, to
keep fighting, and to keep believing, as
Dolores taught us, that ‘‘Sı́, se puede.’’
Angela and I send our deepest condolences to the Huerta family, to her
brothers and sisters in labor, and to all
the lives she touched through her extraordinary life.

community in the State of Georgia.
This Saturday, November 14, the
GHCA will hold its annal gala and kick
off its 15-year anniversary celebration,
and I join executive director Gabriela
Matute, the board of directors, staff,
and supporters in celebrating this exciting anniversary.
Established in 2012, the GHCA has
worked to promote a vibrant construction industry in which Georgia’s Hispanic business are respected, empowered, and have access to opportunities
to thrive.
Their work aims to provide educational and business development resources to construction firms in Georgia, supporting Hispanic entrepreneurs,
creating jobs, and fostering the success
of the Hispanic construction community.
As Georgia’s senior U.S. Senator, I
congratulate and commend the Georgia
Hispanic Construction Association for
their 15 years of devoted service to the
State of Georgia.∑

INTRODUCTION OF BILLS AND
JOINT RESOLUTIONS
The following bills and joint resolutions were introduced, read the first
and second times by unanimous consent, and referred as indicated:
By Ms. DUCKWORTH (for herself and
Mr. DURBIN):
S. 5717. A bill to amend title 36, United
States Code, to move the place of incorporation and domicile of the National Woman’s
Relief Corps to Illinois, to move the principal office of such Corps to Murphysboro, Illinois, and for other purposes; to the Committee on the Judiciary.
By Mrs. FISCHER (for Ms. BLUNT
ROCHESTER (for herself and Mrs.
FISCHER)):
S. 5718. A bill to amend title 49, United
States Code, with respect to restroom access
for certain drivers, and for other purposes; to
the Committee on Commerce, Science, and
Transportation.
f

name of the Senator from New Hampshire (Ms. HASSAN) was added as a cosponsor of S. 1335, a bill to amend the
Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exclude debt held by certain insurance
companies from capital assets and to
extend capital loss carryovers for such
companies from 5 years to 10 years.

‘‘(iv) ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT.—Not
later than 10 days after the date on which an
applicant submits to a certifying authority a
certification application for an individual
Federal license or permit, the certifying authority shall acknowledge receipt of the certification application in writing.
‘‘(v) NOTIFICATION OF COMPLETE APPLICATION OR IDENTIFICATION OF MISSING MATERIALS.—Not later than 90 days after the date
on which a certifying authority acknowledges receipt of a certification application
under clause (iv), the certifying authority
shall—
‘‘(I) provide the applicant a written notification that the certification application is
complete; or
‘‘(II) identify to the applicant in writing
all specific additional materials or information described in clauses (ii) and, if applicable, (iii) necessary for the certification application to be considered complete, including,
for each such additional piece of material or
information, a description of the water quality requirement for which the additional material or information is needed in order to
evaluate compliance with that water quality
requirement.
‘‘(vi) PETITION TO COURT.—
‘‘(I) RIGHT TO PETITION.—An applicant may
petition for judicial review of an alleged failure by a certifying authority to act in accordance with clauses (ii) through (v) by filing a written petition in a court of competent jurisdiction.
‘‘(II) CONSIDERATIONS.—In reviewing a petition under this subclause, a reviewing court
shall consider—
‘‘(aa) the administrative record, which
shall consist of the materials required to be
submitted under clause (ii);
‘‘(bb) any materials or information identified by certifying authority as missing pursuant to a notification under clause (v)(II);
‘‘(cc) the information submitted by the applicant to the certifying authority; and
‘‘(dd) any evidence presented to the court
by the applicant that suggests that the defense of the certifying authority to the petition is pretextual.
‘‘(III) COURT ORDER.—If a court, in reviewing a petition under this clause, finds that a
certifying authority has failed to act in accordance with any of clauses (ii), (iv), and
(v), the court shall provide injunctive relief,
as appropriate, to give effect to this section.
‘‘(D) DENIALS OF CERTIFICATION FOR INDIVIDUAL LICENSE OR PERMIT.—If a certifying
authority denies a certification application
for an individual license or permit, the certifying authority shall provide to the applicant and the applicable Federal licensing or
permitting agency—
‘‘(i) the specific water quality requirements that the certifying authority determined will be violated if certification were
granted;
‘‘(ii) a statement explaining why the certifying authority determined the identified
water quality requirements will be violated;
and
‘‘(iii) if the denial is due to insufficient information, a description of the specific water

‘‘(4) REVIEW PERIOD.—
‘‘(A) IN GENERAL.—Subject to subparagraph
(C) and in consultation with each certifying

‘‘(C) REQUIREMENT FOR EXTENSION.—With

issue a final action on the certification application; and
‘‘(III) a commitment to provide, not less
frequently than monthly, an update on the
status of the review of the certification application.

after the date on which the Secretary determines such failure exists, the Secretary shall
notify such hospital of such determination,
which shall include a request for a corrective
action plan if applicable to comply with such
requirements.
‘‘(B) CIVIL MONETARY PENALTY.—
‘‘(i) IN GENERAL.—In addition to any other
enforcement actions or penalties that may

fails to comply with the requirements of this

on the day the hospital was first out of compliance, as determined by the Secretary)
during which such failure was ongoing. Such

‘‘(I) in the case of a specified hospital with

‘‘(II) in the case of a specified hospital with

$12.50 per bed per day (or, in the case of such
a hospital that has been noncompliant with
such requirements for a 1-year period or
longer, beginning with the first day following such 1-year period, $15 per bed per
day);
‘‘(III) in the case of a specified hospital
with more than 100 beds but fewer than 201
beds, $17.50 per bed per day (or, in the case of
such a hospital that has been noncompliant

longer, beginning with the first day following such 1-year period, $20 per bed per
day);
‘‘(IV) in the case of a specified hospital
with more than 200 beds but fewer than 501
beds, $20 per bed per day (or, in the case of
such a hospital that has been noncompliant
with such requirements for a 1-year period or
longer, beginning with the first day following such 1-year period, $25 per bed per
day); and
‘‘(V) in the case of a specified hospital with
more than 500 beds, $25 per bed per day (or,
in the case of such a hospital that has been
noncompliant with such requirements for a
1-year period or longer, beginning with the
first day following such 1-year period, $35 per
bed per day).
‘‘(ii) INCREASE AUTHORITY.—In applying
this subparagraph with respect to hospitals
that fail to comply in 2028 or a subsequent
year, the Secretary may through notice and
comment rulemaking increase—
‘‘(I) the limitation on the per day amount
of any penalty applicable to a hospital under
clause (i)(I);
‘‘(II) the limitations on the per bed per day
amount of any penalty applicable under any
of subclauses (II) through (V) of clause (i);
and
‘‘(III) the limitation on the increase of any
penalty applied under clause (iii) pursuant to
the amounts specified in subclause (II) of
such clause.
‘‘(iii) PERSISTENT NONCOMPLIANCE.—
‘‘(I) IN GENERAL.—In the case of a hospital
that the Secretary has determined to be noncompliant with the provisions of this subsection two or more times during a 1-year
period (as determined by the Secretary), the
Secretary may increase any penalty otherwise applicable under this subparagraph by
the amount specified in subclause (II) with
respect to such hospital and may require
such hospital to complete such additional
corrective actions plans as the Secretary
may specify.
‘‘(II) SPECIFIED AMOUNT.—For purposes of
subclause (I), the amount specified in this
subclause is, with respect to a hospital—
‘‘(aa) with more than 30 beds but fewer
than 101 beds, an amount that is not less
than $500,000 and not more than $1,000,000;
‘‘(bb) with more than 100 beds but fewer
than 301 beds, an amount that is greater
than $1,000,000 and not more than $2,000,000;

this section to hospitals requesting such assistance.
‘‘(v) APPLICATION OF CERTAIN PROVISIONS.—
The provisions of section 1128A of the Social
Security Act (other than subsections (a) and
(b) of such section) shall apply to a civil
monetary penalty imposed under this subparagraph in the same manner as such provisions apply to a civil monetary penalty imposed under subsection (a) of such section.
‘‘(C) NO AUTHORITY TO WAIVE OR REDUCE
PENALTY.—The Secretary shall not grant or
extend any waiver, delay, tolling, or other
mitigation of a civil monetary penalty for
failing to comply with the requirements of
this subsection except where the Secretary
determines that imposing the maximum
civil monetary penalty, including penalties
for persistent noncompliance, will disrupt
hospital operations in a manner that impacts patient care. The Secretary may request documentation in such form and manner as the Secretary may require in order to
evaluate impact on hospital operations.
‘‘(D) PROHIBITION ON EXTRAORDINARY COLLECTION.—In addition to civil monetary penalties applicable under subparagraph (B) and
any other enforcement actions or penalties
that may apply under any other provision of
law, for a hospital that has received a request for a corrective action plan under subparagraph (A) and fails to comply with the
requirements of this subsection by the date
that is 90 days after such request, that hospital or any other person or entity collecting
on behalf of the hospital shall—
‘‘(i) not take any extraordinary collection
actions against any patient or patient guarantor for debt incurred by any patient on the
date or dates of service when the hospital
was not in compliance with the requirements
of this subsection;
‘‘(ii) cease any extraordinary collection actions that have begun against any patient or
patient guarantor for debt incurred by any
patient on the date or dates of service when
the hospital was not in compliance with the
requirements of this subsection; and
‘‘(iii) not take any extraordinary collection actions against any patient or patient
guarantor for debt incurred by any patient
on the date or dates of service when the hospital was not in compliance with the requirements of this subsection after the hospital
comes back into compliance with the requirements of this subsection.
‘‘(8) RULEMAKING.—
‘‘(A) IN GENERAL.—The Secretary shall implement this subsection through notice and
comment rulemaking in accordance with
section 553 of title 5, United States Code.
‘‘(B) OWNERSHIP INFORMATION.—In promulgating regulations under this paragraph, the
Secretary shall define the individuals and organizations that must be disclosed under
paragraph (1)(C) in a manner that harmonizes disclosure requirements with requirements established under section 1124 of
the Social Security Act and prioritizes the
disclosure of individuals and organizations
who’s ownership or management relationship
with a hospital impacts operational, financial, or clinical decision making for such
hospital.’’.

SEC. l03. CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORY
PRICE TRANSPARENCY.

Section 2718A of the Public Health Service
Act, as added by section l02, is amended by
adding at the end the following:
‘‘(c) CLINICAL DIAGNOSTIC LABORATORY
PRICE TRANSPARENCY.—
‘‘(1) IN GENERAL.—Beginning January 1 of
the year that begins on or after the date that
is 1 year after the date of enactment of the
Patients Deserve Price Tags Act, an applicable laboratory shall, on a quarterly basis (if
there have been any changes to the standard
charges described in paragraph (2)) compile
and make publicly available on an internet
website (without subscription and free of
charge)—
‘‘(A) the standard charges described in
paragraph (2) with respect to each specified
clinical diagnostic laboratory test that such
laboratory so furnishes; and
‘‘(B) the name and business address for
each person or entity that, with respect to
the laboratory—
‘‘(i) has an ownership or investment interest;
‘‘(ii) has a controlling interest;
‘‘(iii) is a management services organization; or
‘‘(iv) is a significant equity investor.
‘‘(2) STANDARD CHARGES DEFINED.—For purposes of paragraph (1), the term ‘standard
charges’ means, with respect to an applicable
laboratory and a specified clinical diagnostic
laboratory test, the following:
‘‘(A) A plain language description of each
item or service, accompanied by any applicable billing codes (including modifiers that
materially change the price for insurers or
providers, and that materially change out-ofpocket costs for consumers) using commonly
recognized billing code sets, including—
‘‘(i) the Healthcare Common Procedure
Coding System code;
‘‘(ii) the National Drug Code; or
‘‘(iii) other applicable identifier as determined by the Secretary (or successor code
sets).
‘‘(B) The gross charge expressed as a dollar
amount, for each such test.
‘‘(C) The discounted cash price.
‘‘(D) The payer-specific negotiated charges,
expressed as a dollar amount and clearly associated with the name of the applicable
third-party payer and name of each plan,
that apply to each such test. If the charges
are based on an algorithm, percentage of another amount, or other formula or criteria,
the applicable laboratory also shall disclose
such algorithm, percentage, formula, or criteria as set forth in its contract and any
other information necessary to determine
the negotiated charge as a dollar amount.
‘‘(E) The de-identified maximum and minimum negotiated charges for each such item
or service, expressed as a non-zero dollar
amount.
‘‘(F) Any other additional information the
Secretary may require for the purpose of improving the accuracy of, or enabling consumers to easily understand and compare,
standard charges for an item or service, except information that is duplicative of any
other reporting requirement under this section. In the case of standard charges for an
item or service included as part of a bundled,
per diem, episodic, or other similar arrangement, the information described in this subparagraph shall be made available as determined appropriate by the Secretary.
‘‘(3) UNIFORM METHOD AND FORMAT.—The
Secretary shall establish a standard, uniform
method and format for applicable laboratories to use in compiling and making public
information pursuant to paragraph (1). Such
method and format shall—

E:\CR\FM\A12NO6.033

S12NOPT1

DMWilson on DSK7X7S144PROD with SENATE

November 12, 2026

‘‘(A) include a machine-readable format (or
a successor technology specified by the Secretary) containing the information described
in paragraph (2) for all specified clinical diagnostic laboratory tests furnished by each
laboratory and the ownership information
described in paragraph (1)(B);
‘‘(B) meet such standards as determined
appropriate by the Secretary in order to ensure the accessibility and usability of such
information; and
‘‘(C) be updated as determined appropriate
by the Secretary, in consultation with stakeholders.
‘‘(4) MONITORING COMPLIANCE.—The Secretary shall, in consultation with the Inspector General of the Department of Health and
Human Services, establish a process to monitor compliance with this subsection. Such
process shall ensure that each applicable laboratory’s compliance with this subsection is
reviewed not less frequently than once every
year.
‘‘(5) INCLUSION OF ANCILLARY SERVICES.—
Any charge for a specified clinical diagnostic
laboratory test furnished by an applicable
laboratory made publicly available in accordance with paragraph (1) shall include the
charge for any ancillary item or service
(such as specimen collection services, specimen transport, centrifugation, aliquoting,
labeling, requisition processing, and standard result reporting services) that would customarily and routinely be furnished by such
laboratory as part of such test, as specified
by the Secretary.
‘‘(6) ATTESTATION.—A senior official from
each clinical diagnostic laboratory (the
Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, or an official of equivalent seniority)
shall attest to the accuracy and completeness of the disclosures, and any other attestations as required by the Secretary, made
in accordance with the clinical laboratory
price transparency requirements based on
criteria established by the Secretary.
‘‘(7) ENFORCEMENT.—
‘‘(A) IN GENERAL.—In the case of an applicable laboratory that fails to comply with
the requirements of this subsection—
‘‘(i) the Secretary shall notify such laboratory of such failure not later than 30 days
after the date on which the Secretary determines such failure exists; and
‘‘(ii) upon request of the Secretary, such
laboratory shall submit to the Secretary,
not later than 45 days after the date of such
request, a corrective action plan to comply
with such requirements.
‘‘(B) CIVIL MONETARY PENALTY.—
‘‘(i) IN GENERAL.—An applicable laboratory
that has received a notification under subparagraph (A)(i) and fails to comply with the
requirements of this subsection by the date
that is 90 days after such notification (or, in
the case of an applicable laboratory that has
submitted a corrective action plan described
in subparagraph (A)(ii) in response to a request so described, by the date that is 90
days after such submission) shall be subject
to a civil monetary penalty of an amount
specified by the Secretary for each day (beginning with the day on which the Secretary
first determined that such laboratory was
not complying with such requirements) during which such failure is ongoing (not to exceed $300 per day).
‘‘(ii) INCREASE AUTHORITY.—In applying
this subparagraph with respect to an applicable laboratory that fails to comply with the
requirements of this subsection in 2028 or a
subsequent year, the Secretary may through
notice and comment rulemaking increase
the limitation on the per day amount of any
penalty applicable to an applicable laboratory under clause (i).
‘‘(iii) APPLICATION OF CERTAIN PROVISIONS.—The provisions of section 1128A of the

SEC. l09. STATE PREEMPTION ONLY IN EVENT
OF CONFLICT.

The provisions of section 2718A of the Public Health Service Act (as added and amended by this title) shall not be construed to supersede any provision of State law which establishes, implements, or continues in effect
any requirement or prohibition related to
health care price transparency, including for
hospitals, clinical diagnostic laboratories,
provider of specified imaging services, and
ambulatory surgical centers (as such terms
are defined in section 2718A(a) of the Public
Health Service Act), except to the extent
that such requirement or prohibition prevents the application of a requirement or
prohibition of such sections (or such amendments). Nothing in this section shall be construed to affect group health plans established under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, or alter the application of section 514 of such Act (29 U.S.C.
1144).

(b)
IDENTIFICATION
OF
PREFERRED
ROUTES.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—
(A) INITIAL IDENTIFICATION.—Not later than
2 years after the date of enactment of this
Act, the Secretary and the Secretary of Energy (referred to in this subsection as the
‘‘Secretaries’’), in coordination with relevant Federal agencies involved in the permitting of offshore generation facilities and
offshore transmission facilities, and in consultation with the entities described in paragraph (3), shall identify preferred routes on
the outer Continental Shelf for transmission
cables and sub-seabed infrastructure (where
such routes have not yet been identified), including—
(i) between offshore generation facilities;
and
(ii) between offshore generation facilities
and optimal points of interconnection with
onshore electric grids.
(B) PERIODIC REVIEW.—Not less frequently
than once every 3 years after the initial
identification of preferred routes in accordance with subparagraph (A), the Secretaries,
in coordination with relevant Federal agencies involved in the permitting of offshore
generation facilities and offshore transmission facilities, and in consultation with
the entities described in paragraph (3),
shall—
(i) determine whether additional preferred
routes are needed; and
(ii) if applicable, identify any additional
preferred routes.
(2) CONSIDERATIONS.—In identifying preferred routes under paragraph (1), the Secretaries shall take into account—
(A) existing rights-of-way and existing subseabed infrastructure;
(B) the optimal points of interconnection
between offshore generation facilities and
onshore electric grids;
(C) impacts on the marine environment, including critical habitats or protected areas,
marine organisms, including protected or endangered species, and other ocean users, including fisheries; and
(D) the best available data on fishing effort, landings value, and vessel transit, including vessel monitoring system and vessel
trip report data maintained by the National
Marine Fisheries Service.
(3) CONSULTATION.—In identifying preferred
routes under paragraph (1), the Secretaries
shall consult with—
(A) each Regional Fishery Management
Council established under section 302 of the
Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and
Management Act (16 U.S.C. 1852) with authority over a fishery that may be affected
by a preferred route;
(B) the Governor of each State that may be
affected by a preferred route;
(C) each Indian Tribe that may be affected
by a preferred route; and
(D) to the extent practicable, representatives of commercial, recreational, and subsistence fishing interests that may be affected by a preferred route.

SEC. 12ll. DEFENSE OF ENVIRONMENT AND
PROPERTY.
(a) NAVIGABLE WATERS.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—Section 502 of the Federal

Water Pollution Control Act (33 U.S.C. 1362)
is amended by striking paragraph (7) and inserting the following:
‘‘(7) NAVIGABLE WATERS.—
‘‘(A) IN GENERAL.—The term ‘navigable
waters’ means the waters of the United
States, including the territorial seas, that
are—
‘‘(i) navigable-in-fact; or
‘‘(ii) permanent, standing, or continuously
flowing bodies of water that form geographical features commonly known as
streams, oceans, rivers, and lakes that are
connected to waters that are navigable-infact.
‘‘(B) EXCLUSIONS.—The term ‘navigable
waters’ does not include (including by regulation)—
‘‘(i) waters that—
‘‘(I) do not physically abut waters described in subparagraph (A); and
‘‘(II) lack a continuous surface water connection to navigable waters;
‘‘(ii) man-made or natural structures or
channels—
‘‘(I) through which water flows intermittently or ephemerally; or
‘‘(II) that periodically provide drainage for
rainfall; or
‘‘(iii) wetlands without a continuous surface connection to bodies of water that are
waters of the United States.’’.
(2) JURISDICTION OF EPA AND CORPS OF ENGINEERS.—Title V of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (33 U.S.C. 1361 et seq.) is
amended—
(A) by redesignating section 520 as section
521; and
(B) by inserting after section 519 the following:
‘‘SEC.

520.

JURISDICTION OF THE ADMINISTRATOR AND SECRETARY OF THE
ARMY.
‘‘(a) EPA AND CORPS ACTIVITIES.—An activ-

ity carried out by the Administrator or the
Corps of Engineers shall not, without explicit State authorization, impinge upon the
traditional and primary power of States over
land and water use.
‘‘(b) AGGREGATION; WETLANDS.—
‘‘(1) AGGREGATION.—Aggregation of wetlands or waters not described in clauses (i)
through (iii) of section 502(7)(B) shall not be
used to determine or assert Federal jurisdiction.
‘‘(2) WETLANDS.—Wetlands described in section 502(7)(B)(iii) shall not be considered to
be under Federal jurisdiction.
‘‘(c) JUDICIAL REVIEW.—If a jurisdictional
determination by the Administrator or the
Secretary of the Army would affect the ability of a State or individual property owner
to plan the development and use (including
restoration, preservation, and enhancement)
of land and water resources, the State or individual property owner may obtain expedited judicial review not later than 30 days
after the date on which the determination is
made in a district court of the United States,
of appropriate jurisdiction and venue, that is
located within the State seeking the review.
‘‘(d) TREATMENT OF GROUND WATER.—
Ground water shall—
‘‘(1) be considered to be State water; and
‘‘(2) not be considered in determining or asserting Federal jurisdiction over isolated or
other waters, including intermittent or
ephemeral water bodies.
‘‘(e) PROHIBITION ON USE OF SIGNIFICANT
NEXUS TEST.—
‘‘(1) DEFINITION OF SIGNIFICANT NEXUS
TEST.—In this subsection, the term ‘significant nexus test’ means an analysis to determine whether a water has a significant nexus

(as defined in subsection (c) of section 328.3
of title 33, Code of Federal Regulations (as in

that date), or any similar analysis.
‘‘(2) PROHIBITION.—Notwithstanding any
other provision of law, the Administrator
may not use a significant nexus test to determine Federal jurisdiction over navigable
waters and waters of the United States.’’.
(3) APPLICABILITY.—Nothing in this subsection or the amendments made by this subsection affects or alters any exemption
under—
(A) section 402(l) of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (33 U.S.C. 1342(l)); or
(B) section 404(f) of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (33 U.S.C. 1344(f)).
(b) APPLICABILITY OF AGENCY REGULATIONS
AND GUIDANCE.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—The following regulations
and guidance shall have no force or effect:
(A) The final rule of the Corps of Engineers

(C) Any subsequent regulation of or guidance issued by any Federal agency that defines or interprets the terms ‘‘navigable
waters’’ or ‘‘waters of the United States’’.
(2) PROHIBITION.—The Secretary of the
Army, acting through the Chief of Engineers,
and the Administrator of the Environmental
Protection Agency shall not promulgate any
rules or issue any guidance that expands or
interprets the definition of navigable waters
unless expressly authorized by Congress.
(c) STATE REGULATION OF WATER.—Nothing
in this section or the amendments made by
this section affects, amends, or supersedes—
(1) the right of a State to regulate waters
in the State; or
(2) the duty of a landowner to adhere to
any State nuisance laws (including regulations) relating to waters in the State.

is amended by striking subsection (a) and inserting the following:
‘‘(a) IN GENERAL.—
‘‘(1) ENTRY BY FEDERAL AGENCY.—A representative of a Federal agency shall only
enter private property to collect information
about navigable waters if the owner of that
property—
‘‘(A) has consented to the entry in writing;
‘‘(B) is notified regarding the date of the
entry; and
‘‘(C) is given access to any data collected
from the entry.
‘‘(2) ACCESS.—If a landowner consents to
entry under paragraph (1), the landowner
shall have the right to be present at the time
any data collection on the property of the
landowner is carried out.’’.
(e) COMPENSATION FOR REGULATORY TAKING.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—If a Federal regulation relating to the definition of ‘‘navigable
waters’’ or ‘‘waters of the United States’’ diminishes the fair market value or economic
viability of a property, as determined by an
independent appraiser, the Federal agency
issuing the regulation shall pay the affected
property owner an amount equal to twice the
value of the loss.
(2) ADMINISTRATION.—Any payment provided under paragraph (1) shall be made from

(b) JOINT RESOLUTIONS OF APPROVAL.—
(1) JOINT RESOLUTION OF APPROVAL DEFINED.—In this subsection, the term ‘‘joint
resolution of approval’’ means a joint resolution the sole matter after the resolving
clause of which is as follows: ‘‘That Congress
approves the imposition of the duty or tariffrate quota with respect to lll, request for

of subsections (b) through (f) of section 152 of
the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2192) apply to

(4) RULES OF THE SENATE AND THE HOUSE OF
REPRESENTATIVES.—This subsection is enacted by Congress—
(A) as an exercise of the rulemaking power
of the Senate and the House of Representatives, respectively, and as such is deemed a
part of the rules of each House, respectively,
but applicable only with respect to the procedure to be followed in that House in the
case of a joint resolution of approval, and supersedes other rules only to the extent that
it is inconsistent with such rules; and
(B) with full recognition of the constitutional right of either House to change the
rules (so far as relating to the procedure of
that House) at any time, in the same manner, and to the same extent as in the case of
any other rule of that House.

LOAD SITE.—The terms ‘‘computational load
operator’’, ‘‘computational load owner’’, and

under section 206 of the Federal Power Act
(16 U.S.C. 824e) to ensure that Regional
Transmission Organizations and Independent
System Operators have processes and procedures in their open access transmission tariffs to curtail computational loads before
reasonably foreseeable energy or operating
reserve shortages trigger shortage or scarcity pricing under the applicable tariff, and
not later than the commencement of an energy emergency alert level EEA 1 (as defined
by the North American Electric Reliability
Corporation) or a higher energy emergency
alert level event applicable to the affected
area, if the computational load has failed to
bring sufficient new generation to the grid to
meet its peak demand, plus a reserve margin,
to address reliability and affordability impacts on other grid users.

Regional Transmission Organization or Independent System Operator shall not include a
computational load subject to curtailment
under paragraph (2) in any Commission-jurisdictional resource adequacy procurement,

that computational load.

set the level of compensation for, any computational load owner or computational load
operator for computational load curtailed

from ratepayers other than computational
load owners and computational load operators.

U.S.C. 824d, 824e) that all rates, charges,
terms, and conditions be just and reasonable
and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.
(6) REQUIREMENT.—As soon as practicable,
and not later than 270 days after the date of
enactment of this Act, the Commission shall
establish replacement rates, terms, and conditions that are consistent with the requirements of paragraphs (2) through (5).

SEC. 2401. DEFINITIONS.

In this title:
(1) APPLICANT.—The term ‘‘applicant’’
means any person that applies for—
(A) a permit under this title; or
(B) a modification to, or a renewal of, a
permit issued under this title.
term
(2)
BENEFICIATION.—The
‘‘beneficiation’’ means—
(A) the crushing and grinding of locatable
mineral ore; and
(B) any processes that are employed to free
the mineral from other constituents, includ-

VerDate Sep 11 2014

November 12, 2026

CONGRESSIONAL RECORD — SENATE

05:19 Nov 13, 2026

Jkt 079060

ing physical and chemical separation techniques.
(3) CASUAL USE.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—The term ‘‘casual use’’
means mineral activities that ordinarily result in no or negligible disturbance of Federal land or resources.
(B) INCLUSIONS.—The term ‘‘casual use’’ includes the collection of geochemical, rock,
soil, or mineral specimens using hand tools,
hand panning, or nonmotorized sluicing.
(C) EXCLUSIONS.—The term ‘‘casual use’’
does not include—
(i) the use of mechanized earth-moving
equipment, suction dredging, or explosives;
(ii) the use of motor vehicles in areas
closed to off-road vehicles;
(iii) the construction of roads or drill pads;
or
(iv) the use of toxic or hazardous materials
or explosives.
(4) CLAIM HOLDER.—The term ‘‘claim holder’’ means a person holding a mining claim,
millsite, or tunnel site that is—
(A) located under the general mining laws;
and
(B) maintained in compliance with the
general mining laws and this title.
(5) CONTROL.—The term ‘‘control’’ means
having the ability to determine the manner
in which an entity conducts mineral activities.
(6) EXPLORATION.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—The term ‘‘exploration’’
means creating a surface disturbance (other
than casual use) to evaluate the type, extent, quantity, or quality of minerals
present.
(B) INCLUSIONS.—The term ‘‘exploration’’
includes mineral activities associated with
sampling, drilling, or developing surface or
underground workings to evaluate locatable
mineral values.
(C) EXCLUSIONS.—The term ‘‘exploration’’
does not include the extraction of mineral
material for commercial use or sale.
(7) FEDERAL LAND.—The term ‘‘Federal
land’’ means any land and any interest in
land that is—
(A) owned by the United States; and
(B) open to location of mining claims
under the general mining laws and this Act.
MINERAL.—The
term
(8)
HARDROCK
‘‘hardrock mineral’’ has the meaning given
the term ‘‘locatable mineral’’ except that—
(A) legal and beneficial title to the mineral
need not be held by the United States; and
(B) paragraph (12)(B) does not apply to this
paragraph.
(9) INDIAN COUNTRY.—The term ‘‘Indian
country’’ has the meaning given the term in
section 1151 of title 18, United States Code.
(10) INDIAN LAND.—The term ‘‘Indian land’’
means land that is—
(A) held in trust for the benefit of an Indian Tribe or member of an Indian Tribe; or
(B) held by an Indian Tribe or member of
an Indian Tribe, subject to a restriction by
the United States against alienation.
(11) INDIAN TRIBE.—The term ‘‘Indian
Tribe’’ has the meaning given the term in
section 4 of the Indian Self-Determination
and Education Assistance Act (25 U.S.C.
5304).
(12) LOCATABLE MINERAL.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—The term ‘‘locatable mineral’’ means any mineral—
(i) the legal and beneficial title to which
remains in the United States; and
(ii) that is not subject to disposition
under—
(I) the Mineral Leasing Act (30 U.S.C. 181
et seq.);
(II) the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 (30
U.S.C. 1001 et seq.);
(III) the Act of July 31, 1947 (commonly
known as the ‘‘Materials Act of 1947’’) (30
U.S.C. 601 et seq.); or

PO 00000

Frm 00038

Fmt 4624

Sfmt 0634

(IV) Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired
Lands (30 U.S.C. 351 et seq.).
(B) EXCLUSIONS.—The term ‘‘locatable mineral’’ does not include any mineral that is—
(i) subject to a restriction against alienation imposed by the United States; and
(ii) held in trust by the United States for,
or owned by, any Indian Tribe or member of
an Indian Tribe.
(13) MINERAL ACTIVITY.—The term ‘‘mineral
activity’’ means any activity on a mining
claim, millsite, or tunnel site, or Federal
land used in conjunction with the activity,
for, relating to, or incidental to, mineral exploration, mining, beneficiation, processing,
or reclamation activities for any locatable
mineral.
(14) OPERATOR.—The term ‘‘operator’’
means—
(A) any person proposing, or authorized by
a permit, to conduct mineral activities
under this title; and
(B) any agent of a person described in subparagraph (A).
(15) PERSON.—The term ‘‘person’’ means—
(A) an individual, Indian Tribe, partnership, association, society, joint venture,
joint stock company, firm, company, corporation, cooperative, trust, consortium, or
other organization; and
(B) any instrumentality of a State or local
government, including any publicly owned
utility or publicly owned corporation of a
State or local government.
(16) PROCESSING.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—The term ‘‘processing’’
means processes downstream of beneficiation
used to prepare locatable mineral ore into
the final marketable product.
(B) INCLUSIONS.—The term ‘‘processing’’ includes smelting and electrolytic refining.
(17) SECRETARY.—The term ‘‘Secretary’’
means the Secretary of the Interior.
(18) SECRETARY CONCERNED.—The term
‘‘Secretary concerned’’ means—
(A) with respect to National Forest System
land, the Secretary of Agriculture, acting
through the Chief of the Forest Service; and
(B) with respect to land managed by the
Bureau of Land Management or other Federal land, the Secretary, acting through the
Director of the Bureau of Land Management.
(19) TEMPORARY CESSATION.—The term
‘‘temporary cessation’’ means a halt in mine
related production activities for a continuous period of not longer than 5 years.
DEGRADATION.—The
term
(20)
UNDUE
‘‘undue degradation’’ means substantial irreparable harm to significant scientific, cultural, or environmental resources on public
land.
Subtitle A—Locatable Mineral Deposits
SEC. 2411. LIMITATION ON PATENTS.
(a) DETERMINATIONS REQUIRED.—Notwith-

standing section 2215 (or the amendments
made by that section), no patent shall be
issued by the United States for any mining
claim, millsite, or tunnel site located under
the general mining laws unless the Secretary
determines that—
(1) a patent application was filed with the
Secretary with respect to the claim not later
than September 30, 1994; and
(2) all requirements applicable to the patent application under law were fully complied with by the date described in paragraph
(1).
(b) RIGHT TO PATENT.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—Subject to paragraph (2)
and notwithstanding subsection (c), if the
Secretary makes the determinations under
paragraphs (1) and (2) of subsection (a) with
respect to a mining claim, millsite, or tunnel
site, the claim holder shall be entitled to the
issuance of a patent in the same manner and
degree to which the claim holder would have
been entitled to a patent before the date of
enactment of this Act.

(2) WITHDRAWAL.—The claim holder shall

court of the United States.
(c) REPEAL.—Section 2325 of the Revised
Statutes (30 U.S.C. 29) is repealed.
