FORT ONTARIO HOLOCAUST REFUGEE SHELTER NATIONAL HISTORICAL PARK ESTABLISHMENT
ACT
The bill (S. 432) to establish the Fort
Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park in the State of
New York as a unit of the National
Park System, and for other purposes,
was ordered to be engrossed for a third
reading, was read the third time, and
passed as follows:
S. 432
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in
Congress assembled,
SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

This Act may be cited as the ‘‘Fort Ontario
Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park Establishment Act’’.
SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.

In this Act:
(1) MAP.—The term ‘‘map’’ means the map
entitled ‘‘Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee
Shelter National Historical Park Proposed
Boundary’’, numbered 962/194,681, and dated
September 2024.
(2) NATIONAL HISTORICAL PARK.—The term
‘‘National Historical Park’’ means the Fort
Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National
Historical Park established by section
3(a)(1).
(3) SECRETARY.—The term ‘‘Secretary’’
means the Secretary of the Interior.
(4) STATE.—The term ‘‘State’’ means the
State of New York.
SEC. 3. ESTABLISHMENT OF FORT ONTARIO HOLOCAUST REFUGEE SHELTER NATIONAL HISTORICAL PARK.
(a) ESTABLISHMENT.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—Subject to paragraph (3),

there is established in the State as a unit of
the National Park System the Fort Ontario
Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park.

PO 00000

Frm 00087

Fmt 4624

Sfmt 0634

(2) PURPOSE.—The purpose of the National
Historical Park is to preserve, protect, and
interpret for the benefit of present and future generations resources associated with
the stories of the 982 refugees from World
War II who were housed at Fort Ontario from
August of 1944 until February of 1946.
(3) CONDITIONS OF ESTABLISHMENT.—
(A) DETERMINATION BY THE SECRETARY.—
The National Historical Park shall not be established until the date on which the Secretary determines that a sufficient quantity
of land or interests in land has been acquired
from land identified as ‘‘Proposed Boundary’’
on the map to constitute a manageable park
unit.
(B) NOTICE.—Not later than 30 days after
the date on which the Secretary makes a determination under subparagraph (A), the
Secretary shall publish in the Federal Register notice of the establishment of the National Historical Park.
(4) MAP.—The map shall be on file and
available for public inspection in the appropriate offices of the National Park Service.
(5) BOUNDARY.—The boundary of the National Historical Park shall include any land
or interests in land acquired by the Secretary under this section.
(b) ADMINISTRATION.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—The Secretary shall administer the National Historical Park in accordance with—
(A) this section; and
(B) the laws generally applicable to units
of the National Park System, including—
(i) sections 100101(a), 100751(a), 100752,
100753, and 102101 of title 54, United States
Code; and
(ii) chapters 1003 and 3201 of title 54, United
States Code.
(2) AGREEMENTS.—
(A) COOPERATIVE AGREEMENTS.—In accordance with section 101702 of title 54, United
States Code, the Secretary may enter into
cooperative agreements with the State or
other public and private entities to provide
interpretive and educational services within
the National Historical Park.
(B) INTERPRETATION AND RESTORATION
AGREEMENTS.—The Secretary may enter into
agreements to identify, interpret, and restore nationally significant historic or cultural resources located on non-Federal land
within the boundary of, or in close proximity
to, the National Historical Park.
(C) PUBLIC ACCESS.—Any cooperative agreement entered into under subparagraph (B) to
provide assistance to non-Federal land shall
provide for reasonable public access to the
non-Federal land.
(3) ACQUISITION OF LAND.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—Subject to subparagraph
(B), the Secretary may acquire land and interests in land located within the boundary
of the National Historical Park by—
(i) donation;
(ii) purchase with donated or appropriated
funds; or
(iii) exchange.
(B) LIMITATION.—Any land owned by the
State or a political subdivision of the State
may be acquired for inclusion in the National Historical Park only by donation.
(4) MANAGEMENT PLAN.—Not later than 3
fiscal years after the date on which funds are
made available to carry out this section, the
Secretary, in consultation with the State,
shall complete a general management plan
for the National Historical Park in accordance with—
(A) section 100502 of title 54, United States
Code; and
(B) any other applicable laws.

HONORING THE LIFE OF JOSEPH
NIEL SPILLANE

HON. JOE COURTNEY
OF CONNECTICUT

rfrederick on LAP6701GR3PROD with REMARKS

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Thursday, November 12, 2026
Mr. COURTNEY. Mr. Speaker, I rise today
to honor the life and legacy of an exemplary
individual, Mr. Joseph Niel Spillane of Mystic,
Connecticut, who passed away on September
18, 2026, at 102 years old.
Niel truly embodied the title of ‘‘public servant.’’ His epic journey included distinguished
military and civilian work for the United States
Armed Forces, elected office and chairmanships of numerous local commissions, and
participation in eastern Connecticut community
organizations and his beloved church. His
generosity and desire to help others knew no
bounds and was a driving impetus clearly reflected in all aspects of his life.
At the start of his impressive career, Niel received undergraduate degrees in both Naval
Architecture and Marine Engineering and
began his graduate studies in Environmental
Engineering. However, before he could receive his master’s degree, he joined the
United States Army. His military service was
expansive, yielding a Bronze Star Medal and
a Presidential Unit Citation after his participation in World War II, where he landed at Normandy and saw heavy combat in the Battle of
the Hedgerows and the Battle of the Bulge.
His Army unit was one of the first cohorts of
United States troops to cross into Germany
during the final push that defeated the Nazi’s
murderous regime. After risking so much in
World War II, he nonetheless once again en-

tered active-duty service during the Korean
War as an officer in the United States Navy
and went on to achieve the rank of Lieutenant
Commander in the United States Navy Reserve.
After the completion of his military service,
Niel utilized his naval education to pursue a
25-year career at General Dynamics Electric
Boat, a cornerstone of eastern Connecticut’s
economy and community. His tenure at EB,
where he rose to the position of Assistant to
the President for Manufacturing, helped yield
the USS Nautilus, the first nuclear-powered
submarine in the world, a creation now instrumental in the military success of the United
States. He then went on to offer his expertise
as the Vice President of ShipTech International, which consulted on shipbuilding operations across the country. Of particular interest, in the late 1950s, Niel was instrumental in
the historic effort by the United States Navy to
assist our ally Great Britain in standing up its
own fleet of nuclear-powered submarines. His
work enabling the transfer of such sensitive
technology is a highly relevant and powerful
example in 2026, as our Nation is engaged in
a similar naval enterprise with our ally Australia.
Niel was drawn back to public service after
his time in the private sector and was welcomed with open arms by his Connecticut
community. He was elected to serve as a
Representative Town Meeting member in both
Waterford and Groton, Connecticut, on the
Waterford Town Council, and finally as Mayor
of Groton. This repertoire of service was
joined as well by his chairmanship and vice
chairmanship of five different local commissions and boards. It is clear by the trust his
neighbors placed in him, that Niel’s desire to
serve others was more than a passion, it was
a calling.
On July 26, 2024, alongside the University
of Connecticut, I had the honor of memorializing Niel’s extraordinary, fascinating and
historic career through the Library of Congress’ Veterans History Project. During our
two hours together, Niel shared stories never
publicly told, recounting both the highlights
and lowlights of his service. Captivated by his
words, the audience listened to his authentic
perspective on service and sacrifice. During
his recounting of being a direct participant in
some of the most consequential events of the
20th century, his down-to-earth modesty and
decency shone through, which made his retelling even more powerful.
In his retirement Niel expressed his creativity as a woodcarver and a caroler, bringing
joy to his town by way of music and the iconic
and beautiful ‘‘Welcome to Historic Mystic’’
signs that mark the entrances to the community.
Whether at the Veteran’s coffeehouse or
SubVets, every opportunity to see Niel allowed
for the rediscovery of long forgotten moments
of our region’s history. It is a privilege to share
just a few highlights from a very full and honorable life of service to others and to our Nation as a whole. I ask that the House join me

in extending our condolences to his children,
Nancy Spillane and Jamie Spillane; to his six
grandchildren; and to his five great-grandchildren.
f

PERSONAL EXPLANATION

HON. RUSSELL FRY
OF SOUTH CAROLINA

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Thursday, November 12, 2026
Mr. FRY. Mr. Speaker, I was unable to cast
my vote concerning the impeachment of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Had I been
present, I would have voted in support of Secretary Hegseth and against these impeachment efforts.
The Constitution grants Congress the authority to impeach civil officers for treason,
bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors. Policy disagreements do not meet
that constitutional threshold. Impeachment is a
serious constitutional responsibility that should
be exercised sparingly, not rushed through
without hearings, public testimony, or due
process.
If House Democrats have demonstrated
anything since last Tuesday, it is that they are
more interested in pursuing impeachment of
President Trump and members of his Cabinet
than delivering meaningful results for the
American people.

Ms. OMAR. Mr. Speaker. I rise today to recognize the Korean Service Center (KSC), on
the occasion of their 35th anniversary. The
KSC has been instrumental in providing essential culturally responsive services to Korean and other immigrant-Americans since its
founding in 1989.
Located in the heart of Minneapolis’ Cedar
Riverside community—the same neighborhood

VerDate Sep 11 2014

06:32 Nov 13, 2026

Jkt 079060

I grew up in—the Korean Service Center was
established when a Minneapolis Public Housing Authority (MPHA) intern identified a gap in
Korean immigrants receiving essential social
services. What initially began as an adjustment program for new Korean immigrants to
learn English and take naturalization classes,
has expanded over decades to provide a variety of holistic programs and support ranging
from new parent education to caregiver consultations and support.
Their presence in the community has built
long-lasting trust and relationships with the
very people they serve; and in 2019, after a
horrific fire in the MPHA’s Cedar High Apartment building, the Korean Service Center staff
were immediately on the scene along with first
responders to assist those impacted—that is a
testament to their unwavering commitment to
community.
As an immigrant, I know how important cultural community organizations like the Korean
Service Center are. These centers serve as
the first point of contact for families who are
seeking resources but may not know where to
start. They provide community enrichment, social services and 24-hour customized living
services both in seniors’ own home and in
their Grace Place facility—which I had the
honor of visiting in 2023. During my visit, I
saw first-hand the incredible services they provide to ensure that Korean immigrants can live
independent and healthy lives without facing
cultural or language barriers. This has earned
them recognitions such as the 2016 Circle of
Excellence Award from the Minnesota Department of Human Services.
In Minnesota, we care for our communities,
and it is evidenced in organizations like the
Korean Service Center. Mr. Speaker, I ask
that my colleagues join me in celebrating the
KSC’s 35th anniversary.

RESHORING AMERICAN
MANUFACTURING ACT OF 2026
SPEECH OF

HON. HALEY M. STEVENS
OF MICHIGAN

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Wednesday, November 11, 2026
Ms. STEVENS. Mr. Speaker, helping American manufacturers bring production home is a
bipartisan goal that should unite this Congress
and the next. H.R. 9718, the Reshoring American Manufacturing Act of 2026, is a welcome
first step toward that goal, helping small businesses find resources and domestic partners.
Connecting businesses with assistance is
valuable, but its effectiveness depends on the
resources available. Congress must build on
the RAM Act by ensuring those resources address the financial and technological barriers
to domestic production.
That need is particularly pressing in critical
materials. China’s dominance in processing
and refining leaves Michigan’s automotive industry and manufacturers nationwide vulnerable to supply disruptions and economic pressures. Building competitive domestic capacity
requires access to capital and investment in
innovation.
My Unearth America’s Future Act would provide that support through loans and loan guarantees, investment and production tax credits,
research and demonstration programs, and a
national supply chain center. These tools
would help expand domestic processing, refining, and recycling capabilities, supporting
American jobs and reducing dependence on
China.
I welcome bipartisan support for the RAM
Act. I urge my colleagues to build on that
commitment by advancing the Unearth America’s Future Act—strengthening the resources
manufacturers need to bring production home.

HONORING THE LIFE AND LEGACY
OF THOMAS H. WHITEMAN, SR.

HON. BILL HUIZENGA
OF MICHIGAN

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Thursday, November 12, 2026
Mr. HUIZENGA. Mr. Speaker, I rise today to
honor the life and legacy of Thomas H. Whiteman, Sr., a devoted husband, father, grandfather, and United States Army veteran who
passed away on November 7, 2026, at the
age of 85.
Born on June 24, 1941, in Gary, Indiana, to
James and Ruby Whiteman, Tom graduated
from La Paz High School in 1961. He went on
to serve our Nation in the United States Army
during the Vietnam War, where he worked as
a soldier, welder, and blacksmith, earning the
rank of Sergeant before receiving an honorable discharge.
On April 15, 1966, Tom married Maxine
Norton, beginning a marriage that would span
more than 60 years. Together, they raised two
sons, Thomas, Jr. and Todd, and built a family
rooted in faith, hard work, and service to others.
Throughout his life, Tom demonstrated remarkable mechanical ability and an entrepreneurial spirit. He and Maxine operated Tom’s
Mobile Service before he began his career as
a millwright, working at Allied Products and
later Bendix. During his 32 years at Bendix,
Tom served as a steward and trustee of
United Auto Workers Local 9, advocating for
his fellow workers until his retirement in 2006.
Tom’s commitment to service extended far
beyond his military career. A longtime member
of Beaver Creek Wesleyan Church, he generously volunteered his talents to repair, build,
and maintain whatever his church family needed. Known for his compassion, resourcefulness, and selflessness, Tom was a man who
preferred helping others to receiving recognition.
Tom is survived by his beloved wife, Maxine; his sons, Thomas, Jr. and Todd; and his
grandchildren. His son Todd serves as my
Chief of Staff, and I have had the privilege of
witnessing firsthand the dedication to service
that continues through the Whiteman family.
Mr. Speaker, Thomas Whiteman exemplified
the values of faith, family, hard work, and
service to country. His life reminds us that a

acts of kindness and generosity that strengthen our families and communities.
I ask my colleagues to join me in honoring

and the entire Whiteman family. May God

Sfmt 9920

Thursday, November 12, 2026
Mr. CARSON. Mr. Speaker, I rise today to
introduce the Asal Sayas National Strategy on
Young Adult Cancers Act, legislation that
would direct the National Institutes of Health
(NIH) to develop a comprehensive national
strategy to address the alarming rise of cancer
among young adults ages 18 to 49.
This legislation is named in honor of Asal
Sayas, a former member of my congressional
staff whose experience with young adult cancer inspired this bill. Asal’s story reflects the
reality faced by far too many young Americans
who confront a devastating diagnosis while
navigating a healthcare system that is often inadequately equipped to recognize, diagnose
and treat cancers in their age group.
Young adult cancer is an urgent and growing public health concern. Since 1990, cancer
incidence among individuals ages 18 to 49
has risen by 79 percent globally. In the United
States, approximately 200,000 young adults
are diagnosed with cancer each year, and
roughly 30,000 lose their lives. Despite these
troubling figures, young adults experience an
average delay of seven months between the
onset of symptoms and treatment, compared
to just one month for adults over 50.
These delays are not simply statistics. They
represent missed opportunities for early detection, timely treatment, and potentially lifesaving
care. Outdated screening guidelines, overlooked symptoms, and gaps in provider
awareness continue to leave young adults vulnerable. Beyond the devastating human toll,
young adult cancers impose an estimated $50
billion to $80 billion in annual economic costs
through medical expenses, lost productivity,
and caregiver responsibilities. These are parents, workers, students, and caregivers whose
lives and futures are being disrupted by a disease that demands greater national attention.
The Asal Sayas National Strategy on Young
Adult Cancers Act takes a comprehensive approach to addressing this growing crisis. The
legislation directs the NIH to develop a national strategy focused on expanding public
and provider education, advancing research,
improving access to screening and early detection, reducing insurance barriers, and supporting innovative treatments. The bill also
calls for the establishment of a National Centers of Excellence for Young Adult Cancers
program through the National Cancer Institute,
creating dedicated hubs for research and clinical care. Additionally, it would establish an
online federal clearinghouse to connect patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers
with critical resources, treatment information,
and ongoing clinical trials.
To ensure accountability and coordination,
the legislation would establish a Federal Coordinating Committee on Young Adult Cancers, bringing together more than 20 federal
agencies and departments, alongside researchers and patient advocates, to oversee
implementation and report progress to Congress.

E:\CR\FM\A12NO8.012

E12NOPT1

November 12, 2026

Mr. Speaker, no young adult should have to
fight for a timely diagnosis or navigate a cancer diagnosis without the resources and support they deserve. By strengthening research,
improving early detection, and coordinating
our Nation’s response, we can work toward a
future where young adults facing cancer have
a better chance at survival and a healthier future.
This legislation honors Asal Sayas and the
countless young Americans whose lives have
been affected by cancer. I urge my colleagues
on both sides of the aisle to join me in advancing the Asal Sayas National Strategy on
Young Adult Cancers Act and reaffirming our
commitment to ensuring that no generation is
overlooked in our Nation’s fight against cancer.

the City of Hilltop, Minnesota, on the occasion
of its 70th anniversary. Hilltop is a community
that has shown the value of resilience, civic
participation, and how the collective strength
of neighbors can create a better future.
Before its founding in 1956, Hilltop was
home to many manufactured housing parks as
the demand for affordable mobile homes increased by the end of WWII. To keep local
control and develop their community during

PO 00000

Frm 00005

Fmt 0626

Sfmt 9920

the fast-paced growth of the Twin-Cities, Hilltop grew from a small, manufactured housing
community into one of Minnesota’s unique municipalities.
Enclaved in the larger City of Columbia
Heights, Hilltop covers about 1/10th of a
square mile and is home to roughly 957 residents. The quaint town’s motto, ‘‘Little City
with a Big Heart,’’ truly encapsulates the essence of the city, as it demonstrates how its
impact is measured not by population or size,
but rather the strength of its residents. Hilltop
has consistently remained dedicated to developing a city that connects people through

being a good neighbor.

in Community Project Funding for Hilltop’s

continue to cultivate a sense of belonging and
community pride. After seven decades, the
City of Hilltop remains a welcoming environment for its residents and visitors.

HONORING THE CAREER AND
SERVICE OF CHERYL FINN

HON. JAMES P. McGOVERN
OF MASSACHUSETTS

IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

Thursday, November 12, 2026
Mr. MCGOVERN. Mr. Speaker. I rise today
in recognition of Cheryl Finn of Uxbridge, Massachusetts, for her remarkable career as a
paramedic, educator, volunteer firefighter, and
leader of global humanitarian relief after 46
years of extraordinary service.
After earning her Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) license in 1979 and her Paramedic Certificate in 1985, Cheryl quickly became a pioneer for women working in the
Emergency Medical Services field. As one of
the first women to work at the Uxbridge Fire
Department, the Bay State Ambulance in
Worcester, and the Auburn Fire Department
ambulance, her strides as an EMT and paramedic blazed a trail for many other women
who have followed.
Cheryl has been a dedicated paramedic and
mentor for decades. She served as the Services Director for the Milford Hospital Paramedic Service as well as the Program Coordinator and Chair of the Quinsigamond Community College Paramedic Program, a position
she held for 25 years. During that entire time,
she continued to work as a paramedic, treating thousands of patients while training and
mentoring hundreds of EMTs and paramedics.
Borders never got in the way of Cheryl’s determination to help people. Guided by her
deep faith, Cheryl has both participated in and
led various trips conducting international medical work. She has provided humanitarian aid
in Tanzania, Zanzibar, Colombia, Guatemala,
the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Mexico, and
other countries across the world. While she
was not stationed abroad, Cheryl rallied members of her community to support families in
other nations, including organizing a food drive
for children in Haiti.
The common thread throughout all the work
Cheryl has done is her unyielding devotion to
helping others. Over the course of her career,
Cheryl helped save and improve countless
lives all over the world. Whether it is volunteering as a firefighter in Central Massachusetts or spending six years working in Mexico
with the Benedictines, Cheryl serves as a reminder of the good we can do in the world
and sets a shining example for all of us to follow.
All while doing this vital work, Cheryl and
her late husband Charles also raised four children—Mary, Theresa, Sarah, and Andrew—
who share in their mother’s deep sense of
faith and public service.
On behalf of the United States Congress
and the people of Massachusetts’ 2nd Congressional District, it is my great honor and
privilege to recognize Cheryl Finn and to thank
her for her dedication, altruism, and service to
our community.
